source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτα ἴδωμεν, πῶς λέγει· ταῦτα θεὸς, φησὶν, ὢν προεῖπε, καὶ πάντως ἐχρῆν γενέσθαι τὸ προειρημένον. θεὸς οὖν τοὺς αὑτοῦ μαθητὰς καὶ προφήτας. μεθ᾿ ὧν συνεδείπνει καὶ συνέπινεν, εἰς τοῦτο περιήγαγεν. ὥστε ἀσεβεῖς καὶ ἀνοσίους γενέσθαι, ὃν ἐχρῆν μάλιστα πάντας ἀνθρώπους εὐεργετεῖν, διαφερόντως δὲ τοὺς ἑαυτοῦ συνεστίους. ἢ ἀνθρώπῳ μὲν ὁ κοινωνήσας τραπέζης οὐκ ἂν ἔτι ἐπεβούλευσε, θεῷ δὲ συνευωχηθεὶς ἐπίβουλος ἐγίνετο; καὶ ὅπερ ἔτι ἀτοπώτερον, αὐτὸς ὁ θεὸς τοῖς συντραπέζοις ἐπεβούλευσε, προδότας καὶ δυσσεβεῖς ποιῶν. καὶ πρὸς ταῦτα δὲ, ἐπεὶ βούλει καὶ τοῖς ἐμοὶ φαινομένοις εὐτελέσι τοῦ Κέλσου ἐπιχειρήμασιν ἀπαντᾶν, τοιαῦτα φήσομεν. ὁ μὲν Κέλσος οἴεται διὰ τοῦτο γίνεσθαι τὸ ὑπό τινος προγνώσεως θεσπισθὲν, ἐπεὶ ἐθεσπίσθη· ἡμεῖς δὲ τοῦτο οὐ διδόντες φαμὲν οὐχὶ τὸν θεσπίσαντα αἴτιον εἶναι τοῦ ἐσομένου, ἐπεὶ προεῖπεν αὐτὸ γενησόμενον, ἀλλὰ τὸ ἐσόμενον, ἐσόμενον ἂν καὶ μὴ θεσπισθὲν, τὴν αἰτίαν τῷ προγινώσκοντι παρεσχηκέναι τοῦ αὐτὸ προειπεῖν. καὶ ὅλον γε τοῦτο ἐν τῇ προγνώσει τοῦ θεσπίζοντος αὐτὸ τυγχάνει· δυνατοῦ (δὲ) ὄντος τοῦδέ τινος γενέσθαι δυνατοῦ δὲ καὶ μὴ γενέσθαι, ἔσται τὸ ἕτερον αὐτῶν τόδε τι. καὶ οὔ φαμεν ὅτι ὁ προγινώσκων, ὑφελὼν τὸ δυνατὸν εἶναι γενέσθαι καὶ μὴ γενέσθαι, οἱονεὶ τοιοῦτόν τι λέγει· τόδε πάντως ἔσται, καὶ ἀδύνατον ἑτέρως γενέσθαι. καὶ τὸ τοιοῦτο φθάνει ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν περὶ τοῦ ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν τινος πρόγνωσιν, εἴτε κατὰ τὰς θείας γραφὰς εἴτε κατὰ τὰς Ἑλλήνων ἱστορίας. καὶ ὁ καλούμενός γε παρὰ τοῖς διαλεκτικοῖς ἀργὸς λόγος, σόφισμα τυγχάνων. οὐκ ἔσται μὲν σόφισμα ὅσον ἐπὶ τῷ Κέλσῳ κατὰ δὲ τὸν ὑγιῆ λόγον σόφισμά ἐστιν. ἵνα δὲ τὸ τοιοῦτο νοηθῇ, ἀπὸ μὲν τῆς γραφῆς χρήσομαι ταῖς περὶ (τοῦ) Ἰούδα προφητείαις ἢ τῇ τοῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν περὶ αὐτοῦ ὡς προδώσοντος προγνώσει· ἀπὸ δὲ τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν ἱστοριῶν τῷ πρὸς τὸν Λάϊον χρησμῷ, συγχωρῶν ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος εἶναι αὐτὸν ἀληθῆ, ἐπεὶ μὴ λυπεῖ τὸν λόγον. περὶ τοῦ Ἰούδα τοίνυν ἐν ἑκατοστῷ καὶ ὀγδόῳ λέγεται ἐκ προσώπου τοῦ σωτῆρος ψαλμῷ, οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· „ὁ θεὸς, τὴν αἴνεσίν μου μὴ παρασιωπήσῃς· ὅτι στόμα ἁμαρτωλοῦ καὶ στόμα δολίου ἐπ᾿ ἐμὲ ἠνοίχθη.“ καὶ τηρήσας γε τὰ ἐν τῷ ψαλμῷ γεγραμμένα εὑρήσεις ὅτι, ὡς προέγνωσται προδώσων τὸν σωτῆρα, οὕτως καὶ αἴτιος ὢν τῆς προδοσίας καὶ ἄξιος τῶν ἐν τῇ προφητείᾳ λεγομένων διὰ τὴν κακίαν αὐτοῦ ἀρῶν. τάδε γὰρ παθέτω „ἀνθ᾿ ὧν, φησὶν, οὐκ ἐμνήσθη τοῦ ποιῆσαι ἔλεος καὶ κατεδίωξεν ἄνθρωπον πένητα καὶ πτωχόν.“ οὐκοῦν ἐδύνατο μνησθῆναι „τοῦ ποιῆσαι ἔλεος“ καὶ μὴ καταδιῶξαι ὃν κατεδίωξε· δυνάμενος δὲ οὐ πεποίηκεν ἀλλὰ προέδωκεν, ὥστε ἄξιος εἶναι τῶν ἐν τῇ προφητείᾳ κατ᾿ αὐτοῦ ἀρῶν. καὶ πρὸς Ἕλληνας δὲ χρησόμεθα τῷ εἰρημένῳ τοῦτον τὸν τρόπον πρὸς τὸν Λάϊον, εἴτε αὐταῖς λέξεσιν εἴτε τὸ ἰσοδυναμοῦν αὐταῖς ἀναγράψαντος τοῦ τραγικοῦ. λέγεται τοίνυν πρὸς αὐτὸν ἀπὸ τοῦ προεγνωκότος δὴ τὰ ἐσόμενα· μὴ σπεῖρε παίδων ἄλοκα δαιμόνων βίᾳ· εἰ γὰρ τεκνώσεις παῖδ᾿, ἀποκτενεῖ σ᾿ ὁ φύς, καὶ πᾶς σὸς οἶκος βήσεται δι᾿ αἱμάτων. καὶ ἐν τούτῳ τοίνυν (σαφῶς) δηλοῦται ὅτι δυνατὸν μὲν ἦν τῷ Λαΐῳ μὴ σπείρειν „παίδων ἄλοκα“· οὐκ ἂν γὰρ τὸ μὴ δυνατὸν προσέταξεν αὐτῷ ὁ χρησμός· δυνατὸν δὲ ἦν καὶ τὸ σπείρειν, καὶ οὐδέτερον αὐτῶν κατηνάγκαστο. ἠκολούθησε δὲ τῷ μὴ φυλαξαμένῳ σπεῖραι „παίδων ἄλοκα“ παθεῖν ἐκ τοῦ ἐσπαρκέναι τὰ τῆς κατὰ Οἰδίποδα καὶ Ἰοκάστην καὶ τοὺς υἱοὺς τραγῳδίας. ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ ἀργὸς καλούμενος λόγος, σόφισμα ὢν, τοιοῦτός ἐστι λεγόμενος ἐπὶ ὑποθέσεως πρὸς τὸν νοσοῦντα καὶ ὡς σόφισμα ἀποτρέπων αὐτὸν χρῆσθαι τῷ ἰατρῷ πρὸς ὑγίειαν, καὶ ἔχει γε οὕτως ὁ λόγος· εἰ εἵμαρταί σοι ἀναστῆναι ἐκ τῆς νόσου, ἐάν τε εἰσαγάγῃς τὸν ἰατρὸν ἐάν τε μὴ εἰσαγάγῃς, ἀναστήσῃ· ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰ εἵμαρταί σοι μὴ ἀναστῆναι ἐκ τῆς νόσου, ἐάν τε εἰσαγάγῃς τὸν ἰατρὸν ἐάν τε μὴ εἰσαγάγῃς, οὐκ ἀναστήσῃ· ἤτοι δὲ εἵμαρταί σοι ἀναστῆναι ἐκ τῆς νόσου ἢ εἵμαρταί σοι μὴ ἀναστῆναι· μάτην ἄρα εἰσάγεις τὸν ἰατρόν. ἀλλὰ χαριέντως τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ τοιοῦτόν τι ἀντιπαραβάλλεται· εἰ εἵμαρταί σοι τεκνοποιῆσαι, ἐάν τε συνέλθῃς γυναικὶ ἐάν τε μὴ συνέλθῃς, τεκνοποιήσεις· ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰ εἵμαρταί σοι μὴ τεκνοποιῆσαι, ἐάν τε συνέλθῃς γυναικὶ ἢ μὴ συνέλθῃς, οὐ τεκνοποιήσεις· ἤτοι δὲ εἵμαρταί σοι τεκνοποιῆσαι ἢ μὴ τεκνοποιῆσαι· μάτην ἄρα συνέρχῃ γυναικί. ὡς γὰρ ἐπὶ τούτου, ἐπεὶ ἀμήχανον καὶ ἀδύνατον τεκνοποιῆσαι τὸν μὴ συνελθόντα γυναικὶ, οὐ μάτην παραλαμβάνεται τὸ συνελθεῖν γυναικί· οὕτως εἰ τὸ ἀναστῆναι ἐκ τῆς νόσου ὁδῷ τῇ ἀπὸ ἰατρικῆς γίνεται, ἀναγκαίως παραλαμβάνεται ὁ ἰατρὸς, καὶ ψεῦδος τὸ „μάτην εἰσάγεις τὸν ἰατρόν.“ ὅλα δὲ ταῦτα παρειλήφαμεν δι᾿ ἃ παρέθετο ὁ σοφώτατος Κέλσος εἰπών· θεὸς ὢν προεῖπε, καὶ πάντως ἐχρῆν γενέσθαι τὸ προειρημένον. εἰ γὰρ τοῦ πάντως ἀκούει ἀντὶ τοῦ κατηναγκασμένως, οὐ δώσομεν αὐτῷ· δυνατὸν γὰρ ἦν καὶ μὴ γενέσθαι. εἰ δὲ τὸ πάντως λέγει ἀντὶ τοῦ ἔσται. ὅπερ οὐ κωλύεται εἶναι ἀληθὲς. κἂν δυνατὸν ᾖ τὸ μὴ γενέσθαι. οὐδὲν λυπεῖ τὸν λόγον· οὐδὲ (γὰρ) ἠκολούθει τῷ προειρηκέναι τὸν Ἰησοῦν (ἀληθῶς) τὰ περὶ τοῦ προδότου ἢ τὰ περὶ τοῦ ἀρνησαμένου τὸ αὐτὸν αὐτοῖς αἴτιον γενέσθαι ἀσεβείας καὶ ἀνοσίου πράξεως. ἰδὼν γὰρ αὐτοῦ τὸ μοχθηρὸν ἦθος ὁ καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς γινώσκων, „τί ἦν ἐν τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ,“ καὶ ὁρῶν ἃ τολμήσει ἔκ τε τοῦ φιλάργυρος εἶναι καὶ ἐκ τοῦ μὴ βεβαίως περὶ τοῦ διδασκάλου φρονεῖν ἃ ἐχρῆν εἶπε μετὰ πολλῶν καὶ τό· „ὁ ἐμβάψας μετ᾿ ἐμοῦ τὴν χεῖρα εἰς τὸ τρυβλίον. ἐκεῖνός με παραδώσει.“
pass_a_gloss: After these let us see how he says: 'these things being god (θεὸς ὤν), he says, he foretold, and by all means (πάντως) it was necessary (χρή) the foretold to happen. God therefore his own disciples (μαθηταί) and prophets (προφῆται), with whom he dined together (συνδειπνέω) and drank together (συμπίνω), led round (περιάγω) to this, so that they became impious (ἀσεβής) and unholy (ἀνόσιος), whom it was necessary most of all to benefit (εὐεργετέω) all men, especially his own hearth-companions (συνέστιοι). Or would one who shared a table (κοινωνέω τραπέζης) with a man no longer plot against him, but one who feasted with (συνευωχέομαι) a god became a plotter (ἐπίβουλος)? And what is still more absurd (ἀτοπώτερον), the god himself plotted against his table-companions (σύντραπεζοι), making [them] traitors (προδόται) and irreverent (δυσσεβεῖς).' And to these, since you wish [me] to meet even Celsus's arguments (ἐπιχειρήματα) that seem to me cheap (εὐτελής), we shall say such things. Celsus thinks that the thing prophesied (θεσπίζω) by some foreknowledge (πρόγνωσις) happens on this account, because it was prophesied; but we, not granting (δίδωμι) this, say that not the prophesier is cause (αἴτιος) of the thing to be, since he foretold it as going to happen, but the thing to be, which would be even if not prophesied, provided (παρέχω) the cause (αἰτία) to the foreknower of foretelling it. And this whole [thing] lies in the foreknowledge of the prophesier: this particular thing being possible (δυνατόν) to happen and possible also not to happen, one (τὸ ἕτερον) of them will be this-particular. And we do not say that the foreknower, removing (ὑφαιρέω) the being-possible to happen and not happen, says as it were something like: this will be by all means and it is impossible to happen otherwise. And such [reasoning] reaches (φθάνω) to all foreknowledge about anything in our power (τὸ ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν), whether according to the divine scriptures (θεῖαι γραφαί) or according to Greek histories. And the so-called among the dialecticians (διαλεκτικοί) lazy argument (ἀργὸς λόγος), being a sophism (σόφισμα), will not be a sophism as far as Celsus goes, but according to sound reasoning (ὑγιὴς λόγος) it is a sophism. That such be understood, from scripture I shall use the prophecies about Judas or the foreknowledge of our Saviour (σωτήρ) about him as about-to-betray; from Greek histories the oracle (χρησμός) to Laius, conceding for the present it is true, since it does not harm the argument. About Judas then in the 108th psalm it is said from the person (πρόσωπον) of the Saviour, whose beginning: 'O God, do not pass over in silence (παρασιωπάω) my praise (αἴνεσις); for mouth of a sinner and mouth of a deceitful (δόλιος) one was opened against me.' Observing (τηρέω) what is written in the psalm you will find that, as he was foreknown as about-to-betray the Saviour, so also being cause (αἴτιος) of the betrayal (προδοσία) and worthy (ἄξιος) of the curses (ἀραί) said in the prophecy because of his wickedness (κακία). Let him suffer these things, 'because, it says, he did not remember to do mercy (ἔλεος) and persecuted (καταδιώκω) a poor (πένης) and beggarly (πτωχός) man'. Therefore he was able to remember 'to do mercy' and not persecute whom he persecuted; being able, he did not do [it] but betrayed, so as to be worthy of the curses in the prophecy against him. And to Greeks we shall use what was said in this manner to Laius, whether in the very words (λέξεις) or the equivalent (ἰσοδυναμοῦν) the tragedian (τραγικός) recorded. It is said to him from the one who foreknew the things to be: 'do not sow (σπείρω) the furrow (ἄλοξ) of children by force (βίᾳ) of the daimones (δαίμονες, gods); for if you beget (τεκνόω) a child, the one born (ὁ φύς) will kill you, and all your house will go through bloods (αἵματα).' And in this then it is clearly shown that it was possible for Laius not to sow 'the furrow of children'; for the oracle would not have commanded (προστάσσω) the impossible; possible also to sow, and neither of them had been necessitated (καταναγκάζω). It followed (ἀκολουθέω) for the one not guarding against sowing to suffer from having sown the [events] of the tragedy about Oedipus and Jocasta and the sons. And the so-called lazy argument, being a sophism, is such, said on hypothesis (ὑπόθεσις) to the sick man (νοσῶν) and as a sophism turning him away from using the physician (ἰατρός) for health (ὑγίεια); the argument goes: if it is fated (εἵμαρται) for you to rise (ἀνίστημι) from the illness, whether you bring in the physician or not, you will rise; if fated not to rise, whether you bring in or not, you will not rise; either it is fated to rise or fated not; in vain (μάτην) then you bring in the physician. But gracefully (χαριέντως) against this argument such a thing is set alongside (ἀντιπαραβάλλω): if fated for you to beget children (τεκνοποιέω), whether you come together (συνέρχομαι) with a woman or not, you will beget; if fated not, whether or not, you will not; either fated to beget or not; in vain then you come together with a woman. For as in this, since it is impossible (ἀμήχανον καὶ ἀδύνατον) for one not coming together with a woman to beget, coming together is not taken up in vain; so if rising from illness happens by the way (ὁδός) of medicine (ἰατρική), the physician is necessarily (ἀναγκαίως) taken up, and false the 'in vain you bring in the physician'. All these we have taken up on account of what the most wise Celsus set forth saying: being god he foretold, and by all means it was necessary for the foretold to happen. For if he hears 'by all means' instead of 'by necessity' (κατηναγκασμένως), we will not grant him; for it was possible also not to happen. But if he says 'by all means' instead of 'it will be', which is not prevented from being true, even if not-happening be possible, it harms (λυπέω) the argument nothing; for neither did it follow (ἀκολουθέω) from Jesus having (truly) foretold the things about the traitor or about the denier that he became for them cause of impiety (ἀσέβεια) and unholy deed (ἀνόσιος πρᾶξις). For seeing his wicked (μοχθηρός) character (ἦθος), the one according to us knowing 'what was in the man', and seeing what he will dare (τολμάω) from being money-loving (φιλάργυρος) and from not thinking firmly (βεβαίως) about the teacher what was necessary, said with many [things] also this: 'the one having dipped (ἐμβάπτω) with me the hand into the dish (τρυβλίον), that one will betray (παραδίδωμι) me.'
pass_b_english: After this let us see how he puts it. “He foretold these things,” he says, “being a god, and what was foretold certainly had to happen. So a god brought his own disciples and prophets, with whom he dined and drank, to the point of becoming impious and unholy, when he above all ought to have done good to all men, and especially to those who shared his table. Or would one who had shared a man’s table not afterwards plot against him, while one who had feasted with a god became his plotter? And, what is still more absurd, the god himself plotted against those at table with him, by making them traitors and impious men.”

Since you wish me to answer even those arguments of Celsus that seem to me trivial, we shall say this in reply. Celsus thinks that what is prophesied by some kind of foreknowledge comes to pass because it was prophesied. We do not grant this. We say that the one who prophesied is not the cause of what will be on the ground that he foretold it would happen; rather, what will be, which would have been even if it had not been prophesied, gave the one who foreknew it the cause for foretelling it. And all of this lies within the foreknowledge of the one who prophesies it: when it is possible for a given thing to happen and possible also for it not to happen, one particular one of the two will come about. And we do not say that the one who foreknows takes away the possibility of its happening or not happening and says, as it were, something like this: “This will certainly be, and it cannot turn out otherwise.” This principle extends to all foreknowledge of anything that lies in our power, whether in the divine Scriptures or in the histories of the Greeks. And what the logicians call the “lazy argument”, which is a sophism, will not be a sophism as far as Celsus is concerned; but by sound reasoning it is a sophism.

To make this understood, I shall use from Scripture the prophecies about Judas, or our Saviour’s foreknowledge of him as the one who would betray him; and from the Greek histories, the oracle given to Laius, granting for the present that it is true, since that does not harm the argument. Concerning Judas, then, the hundred and eighth Psalm (Psalm 109 in English Bibles) speaks in the person of the Saviour; it begins: “O God, do not pass over my praise in silence; for the mouth of a sinner and the mouth of a deceitful man have been opened against me” (Psalm 109:1–2). If you observe what is written in the psalm, you will find that, just as he was foreknown as the one who would betray the Saviour, so he was also the cause of the betrayal, and because of his wickedness deserved the curses spoken in the prophecy. For let him suffer these things, it says, “because he did not remember to show mercy, and persecuted a poor and needy man” (Psalm 109:16). So he could have remembered “to show mercy” and not persecuted the one whom he persecuted; but though he could, he did not do so, and betrayed him instead, so that he deserves the curses pronounced against him in the prophecy.

Against the Greeks we shall use what was said in this way to Laius, whether the tragic poet set it down in its very words or in words of equal force. It is said to him, then, by the one who indeed foreknew what would be: “Do not sow the furrow of children against the will of the gods; for if you beget a child, the one born of you will kill you, and all your house will walk through blood” (Euripides, Phoenician Women 18–20). In this too, then, it is clearly shown that it was possible for Laius not to sow “the furrow of children”, for the oracle would not have commanded him what was not possible; and it was also possible for him to sow, and neither of the two was forced upon him. But because he did not take care not to sow “the furrow of children”, it followed from his having sown that he suffered the tragedy of Oedipus and Jocasta and their sons.

The so-called lazy argument too, which is a sophism, is of this sort: it is put hypothetically to a sick man and, as a sophism, dissuades him from using a physician to regain his health. The argument runs like this: “If it is fated for you to recover from the illness, you will recover whether you call in the physician or not. But if it is fated for you not to recover from the illness, you will not recover whether you call in the physician or not. Now either it is fated for you to recover from the illness or it is fated for you not to recover. Therefore you call in the physician in vain.” But against this argument something like the following is wittily set: “If it is fated for you to beget children, you will beget children whether you lie with a woman or not. But if it is fated for you not to beget children, you will not beget children whether you lie with a woman or not. Now either it is fated for you to beget children or not to beget them. Therefore you lie with a woman in vain.” For just as in this case, since it is out of the question, indeed impossible, that a man who has not lain with a woman should beget children, lying with a woman is not resorted to in vain, so, if recovery from illness comes by way of medicine, the physician is necessarily called in, and it is false that “you call in the physician in vain.”

We have brought in all this because of what the most wise Celsus set down when he said: “Being a god, he foretold, and what was foretold certainly had to happen.” If by “certainly” he means “under compulsion”, we shall not grant it to him, for it was possible for it not to happen as well. But if he says “certainly” in the sense of “it will be”, which nothing prevents from being true even though it is possible for it not to happen, this does no harm to the argument. For it did not follow from Jesus’ having truly foretold what concerned the traitor, or what concerned the one who denied him, that he himself became the cause of their impiety and unholy deed. He who, as we hold, knew “what was in man” (John 2:25) saw the traitor’s wicked character, and saw what he would dare because he loved money and did not hold firmly to what he ought to think about his teacher; and so, among many other things, he said this too: “He who has dipped his hand with me in the dish, he will betray me” (Matthew 26:23).

choices.why: πάντως rendered 'certainly' instead of the calque 'by all means', in both Celsus quotations, in 'This will certainly be', and in Origen's discussion of the word
περιήγαγεν: 'led ... to this point, that they became' -> 'brought ... to the point of becoming'
οὐκ ἂν ἔτι ἐπεβούλευσε: 'no longer plot' -> 'not afterwards plot' (no earlier plotting implied)

choices.term: is not the cause of what will be because he foretold
choices.why: ambiguous 'is not the cause of what will be because he foretold' -> 'on the ground that he foretold'
τὸ ἕτερον αὐτῶν τόδε τι: 'one or the other of the two will be the case' -> 'one particular one of the two will come about'

added '(Psalm 109 in English Bibles)' beside Origen's 'hundred and eighth Psalm'; 'do not keep silent at my praise' -> 'do not pass over my praise in silence' (παρασιωπήσῃς); 'a man poor and needy' -> 'a poor and needy man'
Euripides quotation: 'a son' -> 'a child' (παῖδ᾿); 'the one you beget' -> 'the one born of you' (ὁ φύς); 'wade' -> 'walk' (βήσεται; no added image)
lazy argument: dropped the false comparison 'So too ... of this kind' (τοιοῦτός ἐστι introduces the argument that follows); 'sophistically' -> 'as a sophism' (ὡς σόφισμα)
restored the ὡς γὰρ ... οὕτως structure ('For just as ... so') in the begetting/physician comparison; ἀμήχανον καὶ ἀδύνατον 'out of the question, indeed impossible'

choices.term: did not think steadfastly about his teacher as he ought
choices.why: 'did not think steadfastly about his teacher as he ought' -> 'did not hold firmly to what he ought to think about his teacher'

translator_notes: LXX renumbering: Origen’s ‘hundred and eighth Psalm’ (LXX 108) is Psalm 109 in English Bibles; the opening quoted is LXX 108:1b–2a = Psalm 109:1–2 (the title verse is not counted in English numbering), and ‘because he did not remember to show mercy...’ is LXX 108:16 = Psalm 109:16. The wording ‘in the hundred and eighth Psalm’ is kept as Origen wrote it; the parenthetical gives the English number. The Laius oracle is Euripides, Phoenissae 18–20 (Origen: ‘the tragic poet’); Euripides reads τέκνων ἄλοκα and δι᾿ αἵματος where Origen’s text has παίδων ἄλοκα and δι᾿ αἱμάτων, which fits Origen’s own caveat ‘whether in the very words or their equivalent’. δαιμόνων βίᾳ: ‘against the will of the gods’ (pagan gods, lower case). The ‘lazy argument’ (ἀργὸς λόγος) is the Stoic school name for this fatalist sophism; the ‘witty’ counter-argument (the begetting case) is the one Chrysippus is reported to have used, but Origen names no source, so none is given inline. Staged punctuation breaks several sentences (‘προφήτας. μεθ᾿ ὧν’, ‘ἔσται. ὅπερ’, ‘ἀληθὲς. κἂν’, ‘γενέσθαι. οὐδὲν’, ‘τρυβλίον. ἐκεῖνός’); read continuously. Editorial supplements in round brackets in the staged text, (δὲ), (τοῦ), (σαφῶς), (γὰρ), (ἀληθῶς), are read as part of the text. ‘Since you wish’ (βούλει) addresses Ambrose, the dedicatee. θεός in Celsus’s quoted words rendered ‘a god’, ‘the god himself’ (house convention); ‘his disciples and prophets’ is as the Greek has it. Matthew 26:23 cited for ‘he who has dipped his hand with me in the dish’ (the wording is Matthew’s, with ἐκεῖνος for οὗτος); compare Mark 14:20. ‘Knew what was in man’: John 2:25 (Origen keeps the article τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ). φιλάργυρος may allude to John 12:6 (Judas the thief); not explicit enough to cite inline. Matthew 26:23 has ἐν τῷ τρυβλίῳ; Origen’s εἰς τὸ τρυβλίον is a minor variant of no consequence.
